extracted.intended_audience: Referees/reviewers for MAA journals (The American Mathematical Monthly, Mathematics Magazine, The College Mathematics Journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for referees evaluating submissions to MAA expository mathematics journals, focusing on mathematical correctness, exposition aimed at non-specialist mathematicians, and preparing a thorough referee report to assist editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-anonymous review system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board of Governors of the Mathematical Association of America has mandated that our journals use a double‐anonymous review system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should be aware the journals operate under double‑anonymous review (both author and referee identities concealed). The page states the policy but does not give operational steps here; follow the journal's Editorial Manager instructions for maintaining anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and prohibition on entering manuscripts into external tools (AI policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must keep the manuscript files confidential and must not enter unpublished manuscript files into databases or tools, including generative AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must not use any third party tool to generate their reviewer report (e.g., ChatGPT). When uploading a report referees must confirm: "I confirm I have not uploaded the unpublished manuscript into an AI tool nor have I used an AI tool to provide my reviewer report." The journal may reject reports suspected of violating this policy. The MAA follows Taylor & Francis' AI policy (link provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary role: help the editor determine disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Your primary role as a referee is to help the editor determine how to proceed with the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus reports on assessment and recommendation for the editor (accept, revise, reject, transfer). Comment on general problems apparent in the article. Do not act as the final certifier of content nor as a ghostwriter for the author; offer constructive guidance to inform the editor's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check mathematical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are asked to review the articles and notes to help ensure that the math is accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check proofs, computations, and stated results for correctness. Flag errors and gaps. Although referees should point out inaccuracies, the author remains ultimately responsible for the correctness of the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for inviting exposition and appropriate target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: All articles and notes should be inviting to most readers; making articles inviting usually means aiming them at the right audience, which ought to be mathematicians who are novices in the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the exposition addresses an intelligent non-specialist mathematician (e.g., 'the algebraist down the hall' or a graduate student). Even advanced articles can be inviting if they are accessible to such readers. Comment if background, explanations, or exposition should be adjusted to fit the journal's broad mathematical readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer constructive suggestions, not rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are encouraged to offer constructive suggestions but not to serve as boards of certification or as ghostwriters for careless authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide actionable, prioritized suggestions rather than reauthoring sections. Point out conceptual or structural issues and suggest remedies, but do not rewrite large portions or perform editorial work that is the author's responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a brief summary of the paper (Summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a brief summary of what the article is about, and its relationship to the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the report with a concise summary statement describing main results/ideas and situating the work relative to prior literature; this helps the editor and provides evidence you understood the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: General assessment questions (General Remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a short paragraph or two with your general take on the paper, addressing core evaluative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly address questions such as: Do you think it is interesting? What is good about the paper? Is it appropriate for the journal to which it was submitted or another journal? Is it too long? Is it well‑written? Is the work sufficiently original to merit publication? Are you recommending it for acceptance or not? Use these to frame your overall recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main Suggestions (big-picture revisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any big picture items you would like to see fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List substantive conceptual, structural, or mathematical issues that must be addressed for the paper to be publishable. Prioritize and be specific about what changes are required for acceptance or major revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor Improvements (detailed, page-level suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect suggestions for minor improvements listed by (page, paragraph, line), and other smaller comments for authors to address prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise, line‑level notes (page/paragraph/line) for typos, unclear sentences, small corrections, notation inconsistencies, and bibliography issues. These are for polishing the manuscript after major issues are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: References (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: References may be included in the report (optional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recommending additional or corrective references, list them. This section is optional but helpful when the referee knows relevant prior work that should be cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and review schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask that you send us your referee report within six weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need more time contact publications@maa.org. Reminder policy: if you have not responded, reminders go out after 7 days and 20 days; after that you may be un‑invited. If you agreed to review and miss the due date, reminders are sent 7 and 20 days after the due date and the editor may contact you personally or un‑invite you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting alternate referees and maintaining availability
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are unable to referee please suggest other people whom we could invite; if you no longer want to referee, notify the Publications Department so you can be marked inactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When declining, provide names of suitable alternative referees. If you wish to stop receiving invitations, inform publications@maa.org so your status can be updated in Editorial Manager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of referee responsibility vs author/editor responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: While referees should point out problems, the author is responsible for style and grammar and the editor is responsible for rejecting seriously flawed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel obliged to correct all stylistic or usage issues; focus referee effort on mathematical correctness, clarity of exposition, originality, and suitability for the journal. Recommend rejection for seriously flawed work rather than attempting to salvage it by exhaustive rewrites.
